### Before you start {#before-start}

From Week 10, you should be able to open an R script, find a CSV relative to
your project folder, recognize `NA`, and explain that a service event and a
building are different observation units. You should have seen string cleaning,
factors, timestamps and joins; you do not need to memorize their syntax.
The join examples recall Week 10 and explain why checkpoints matter. You do
not need to write or run a join to complete this chapter.
Use the [post–Week 10 recovery page](https://lnajman.github.io/math346/weeks/recovery-after-week-10.html)
if those ideas are unfamiliar. The complete setup below rebuilds the data;
no saved Week 10 workspace is needed.

::: {.callout-note #words}
## Words used in this chapter

| Word or pattern | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| **Invariant** | A promise that should remain true at a particular stage, such as one row per original event. |
| **Contract** | What a function accepts, what it returns, and when it should stop with an error. |
| **Known-answer test** | A small example whose answer you work out independently before running the code. |
| **Boundary** | The exact dividing value in a rule, such as 12 in a 12-hour target. |
| **Observation key / matching key** | An observation key identifies one row's event; a matching key connects it to another table. Several events can share a matching building key. |
| **Unmatched key** | A key value with no matching row in the other table. |
| **Left join / inner join** | A left join keeps every left-hand row; an inner join keeps only matching rows. Multiple matches can multiply rows in either. |
| **`anti_join(x, y, by = ...)`** | Show rows of `x` with no match in `y` using the stated key. |
| **Many-to-one declaration** | Require each left-hand row to match at most one right-hand row; zero matches are allowed. |
| **`tryCatch`** | Catch an expected error and keep it as an object so the script can continue. |
| **`inherits(x, "error")`** | Ask whether `x` is an error object; the answer is `TRUE` or `FALSE`. |
| **`identical` / `all.equal`** | `identical` checks exact type and value. `all.equal` allows numerical tolerance and returns `TRUE` or a description of differences; use `isTRUE(all.equal(...))` in a check. |

The [course glossary](https://lnajman.github.io/math346/resources/glossary.html)
provides further background.
:::

### Read / Explain / Check / Interpret

Read the inputs and operations; explain your prediction; check a specific
claim; interpret the result with its population, domain or units. Apply this
to supplied code, your own code and LLM-generated code alike.

Think first; write a private comment only where requested—see the
[prediction guide](how-to-use.html#read-explain-check-interpret).

## Start with the familiar data {#setup}

**Slide cue:** “Reuse Familiar Data”.

Download the [synthetic service-event CSV](downloads/week10-service-events.csv),
the [pipeline starter](downloads/week11-readable-pipeline.R), and the
[function starter](downloads/week11-function-contracts.R). Save them as follows:

```text
week11/
  week11-readable-pipeline.R
  week11-function-contracts.R
  data/
    week10-service-events.csv
```

Open this folder as your RStudio project or set it as your working directory.
Use R 4.1 or later and the already-required `readr`, `dplyr`, `stringr` and
`lubridate` packages. If setup is blocked, use the
[course software checks](https://lnajman.github.io/math346/resources/software-requirements.html)
and ask for help; you can still predict outputs while access is resolved.

### Setup check

Run this check from the `week11/` folder before loading packages. It checks the
two starters and the CSV's position without running or changing their contents.
If it lists missing paths, fix those paths before continuing.

```{r}
#| label: setup-files
setup_files <- c(
  "week11-readable-pipeline.R",
  "week11-function-contracts.R",
  "data/week10-service-events.csv"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: author-setup-files
#| include: false
# Author render uses the same public files in the download bundle.
setup_files <- file.path("downloads", basename(setup_files))
```

```{r}
#| label: setup-check
#| output: false
missing_files <- setup_files[!file.exists(setup_files)]
if (length(missing_files) == 0) {
  cat("Setup OK\n")
} else {
  cat("Missing from the current folder:\n",
      paste(missing_files, collapse = "\n"), "\n", sep = "")
}
```

**Example output when all required files are present:**

```text
Setup OK
```

This is example output, not confirmation of your computer's setup. Run the
check in your own R session and inspect that result.

If you see missing paths, run `getwd()` to see where R is looking. Creating a
folder in a file browser does not automatically make it R's working directory.

The starter files contain unfinished tasks. Complete the selected blocks before
running the whole starter. The worked blocks in this chapter run **in order in a
fresh R session**. Closed reveals contain runnable reference code: after your
attempt, open and run them when following the full route. To begin directly
with Meeting 2, run the setup and import below, define
[`within_target`](week-11-meeting-2.html#vector-function), then run the [Meeting 2 setup](week-11-meeting-2.html#meeting-two-setup).
The later original-versus-refactored comparison also needs Meeting 1's stages.

```{r}
#| label: import
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(lubridate)

# In your week11 folder, use the data/ path below.
events_path <- "data/week10-service-events.csv"
```

```{r}
#| label: author-render-path
#| include: false
# The review project stores its supplied CSV in downloads/.
# This author-only path adjustment does not appear in the student example.
events_path <- "downloads/week10-service-events.csv"
```

```{r}
#| label: read-events
stopifnot(file.exists(events_path))
events_raw <- read_csv(
  events_path,
  col_types = cols(
    event_id = col_character(),
    building_key = col_character(),
    reported_at = col_character(),
    issue_label = col_character(),
    severity = col_character(),
    response_hours = col_double()
  ),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
stopifnot(
  nrow(events_raw) == 9,
  !anyNA(events_raw$event_id),
  n_distinct(events_raw$event_id) == 9,
  nrow(problems(events_raw)) == 0
)
dim(events_raw)
```

### What a failed check looks like

A silent `stopifnot` means all its conditions passed. An error names the first
failing condition. The next example deliberately asks for eight rows when the
file has nine; it does not alter `events_raw`.

`tryCatch` catches this expected error and keeps it in `failed_check`, so the
rest of the script can continue. `conditionMessage` reads its message.

```{r}
#| label: failed-check-demo
failed_check <- tryCatch(
  stopifnot(nrow(events_raw) == 8),
  error = function(e) e
)
cat("Error: ", conditionMessage(failed_check), "\n", sep = "")
stopifnot(inherits(failed_check, "error"))
```

The displayed message comes from the actual failed assertion. The final check
passes because the deliberately incorrect assertion produced an error object.
For an unexpected failure, inspect the named condition and its input before
changing anything; deleting the check only hides the problem.

Tables in this chapter display checked output; in R, use `print(object_name)`
to inspect an object. The import output is nine rows and six columns. Each row is **one service event**;
`event_id` identifies that event. A building may have several events. All
response times in this small supplied file are observed; none equals exactly
12 hours. We will therefore need deliberately chosen tests for missingness and
the boundary. These data are synthetic and contain no student information.

## Three distinctions to keep straight {#bridge}

**Slide cue:** “Check The Observation Unit”.

Keep counts separate from identity, an observation key separate from a matching
key, and an unmatched event separate from a lost event.

**Predict before revealing:** a pipeline begins with `E1, E2, E3` and ends
with `E1, E1, E3`. What does a row-count check miss? What if the result is
`E1, E2, E4` instead? Write your prediction in a comment before opening the reveal.

<details>
<summary>Compare your explanation</summary>

Both results still have three rows. The first duplicates E1 and loses E2.
The second has three distinct IDs but replaces E3 with E4. Check the count,
uniqueness **and the original set of IDs**. These are examples of corrupted
processing, not claims that a left join itself drops a left-hand row.

**If your answer differed, the likely cause is** counting rows without checking
which IDs they contain. `E1, E1, E3` also needs a uniqueness check;
`E1, E2, E4` passes uniqueness but fails comparison with the original ID set.

</details>

| Question | Evidence to inspect | What this check does not show |
|---|---|---|
| Are the same events present once each? | Row count, nonmissing unique `event_id`, and the same original ID set | That the attached building information is correct |
| Can several events share a building? | Event identity is `event_id`; raw `building_key` becomes the normalized `building_id` during cleaning and is used for matching | That a registry may contain duplicate building keys |
| Did every event find building information? | Unmatched keys, for example from `anti_join` | That every missing attached field necessarily indicates an unmatched key |
| Does a many-to-one join declaration suffice? | It guards against an event matching multiple registry rows | That every event matches, or that the chosen keys identify the correct building and period |

An unmatched event survives a left join, with missing attached registry fields.
An inner join would exclude it. Investigate that distinction before deleting
rows. Week 11 makes this reasoning easier by keeping named tables before and
after a transformation. We do not repeat the full Week 10 join lab here.

## Meeting 1 · Read the pipeline {#pipeline}

**Slide cues:** “Read A Pipe Top To Bottom”, “What Moves Through The Pipe?”
and “Nested Calls”.

### Follow the whole object

**Predict · Think first:** the number of rows and columns after each call.

```{r}
#| label: trace-pipe
trace_example <- events_raw |>
  transmute(event_id, response_hours) |>
  arrange(event_id)
dim(trace_example)
```

`events_raw` is the first argument of `transmute`. Its nine-row, two-column
result becomes the first argument of `arrange`. The pipe does not mean “run
separately on every row.” `arrange` orders rows; it does not summarize them.
The equivalent nested expression is:

```{r}
#| label: nested-equivalence
trace_nested <- arrange(
  transmute(events_raw, event_id, response_hours),
  event_id
)
stopifnot(identical(trace_example, trace_nested))
```

A shorter expression is useful only if its meaning is easier to inspect. A
long pipe that cleans, joins and summarizes can hide where its promises change.

### Name the state, then check its promise {#checkpoints}

**Slide cues:** “Use Named Checkpoints”, “Name The Data State” and
“Check The Observation Unit”.

Our four states are:

| State | One row represents | Expected size for this file | A useful check |
|---|---|---|---|
| `events_raw` | One supplied service event | 9 × 6 | Import problems and unique nonmissing event IDs |
| `events_clean` | The same event, with normalized fields | 9 × 6 | Same IDs, valid timestamps and ordered severity |
| `events_analysis` | The same event, with derived variables | 9 × 8 | Same IDs, logical flags and correct units |
| `issue_summary` | One issue category | 4 × 5 | Category counts account for all nine events |

Try the selected cleaning checkpoint in your starter first. Then read this
worked block line by line:

```{r}
#| label: clean-events
events_clean <- events_raw |>
  transmute(
    event_id,
    building_id = str_to_upper(str_squish(building_key)),
    reported_at = ymd_hm(reported_at, tz = "Europe/Paris", quiet = TRUE),
    issue = str_to_lower(str_squish(issue_label)),
    severity = factor(
      str_to_lower(str_squish(severity)),
      levels = c("low", "medium", "high"),
      ordered = TRUE
    ),
    response_hours
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(events_clean) == nrow(events_raw),
  !anyNA(events_clean$event_id),
  n_distinct(events_clean$event_id) == nrow(events_clean),
  setequal(events_raw$event_id, events_clean$event_id),
  !anyNA(events_clean$reported_at),
  !anyNA(events_clean$severity),
  is.ordered(events_clean$severity),
  identical(levels(events_clean$severity), c("low", "medium", "high")),
  is.numeric(events_clean$response_hours)
)
```

`transmute` keeps the named output columns. `str_squish` removes surrounding
space and compresses repeated internal spaces; case normalization assumes case
does not distinguish these identifiers or labels. The original table remains
available for inspection. `Europe/Paris` is the synthetic data's time-zone
convention, not the location or time zone of the class. An unknown severity
label can turn into `NA` during factor conversion; inspect the raw text if
that assertion fails.

**Explain:** why do we need both `setequal` and a uniqueness check?

<details>
<summary>Check the reasoning, then damage a copy</summary>

A set ignores repetition. `setequal(c("E1", "E2"), c("E1", "E1", "E2"))`
is true. Set equality checks which IDs are present; uniqueness and row count
check how often they appear. Neither verifies every attached value.

```{r}
#| label: damaged-copy
bad <- events_clean
bad$event_id[2] <- bad$event_id[1]
data.frame(
  rows = nrow(bad),
  distinct_ids = n_distinct(bad$event_id),
  same_ids = setequal(events_raw$event_id, bad$event_id)
)
stopifnot(
  nrow(bad) == 9,
  n_distinct(bad$event_id) == 8,
  !setequal(events_raw$event_id, bad$event_id)
)
```

The result is 9 rows, 8 distinct IDs and `FALSE` for the same-ID test.
`events_clean` is untouched. These assertions verify the deliberately damaged
example; they are not acceptance checks for a cleaned production table.

</details>

### State the target rule before calculating

**Slide cues:** “Add The Target Rule” and “Check The Derived Variable”.

Our flag means **a recorded response at or below 12 hours**. Exactly 12 counts.
A missing response is not evidence that the target was met, so its flag is
`FALSE`. That does **not** establish that the response was late.

**Predict in a comment first:** the flags for 11, 12, 13 and a missing response.
Then open and run the derivation before continuing to the summary.

<details>
<summary>Compare the four flags and run the derivation</summary>

```{r}
#| label: derive-target
x <- c(11, 12, 13, NA_real_)
!is.na(x) & x <= 12

events_analysis <- events_clean |>
  mutate(
    within_12_hours = !is.na(response_hours) & response_hours <= 12,
    response_days = response_hours / 24
  )
stopifnot(
  nrow(events_analysis) == nrow(events_clean),
  identical(events_analysis$event_id, events_clean$event_id),
  is.logical(events_analysis$within_12_hours),
  !anyNA(events_analysis$within_12_hours),
  sum(events_analysis$within_12_hours) == 5,
  isTRUE(all.equal(events_analysis$response_days,
                  events_clean$response_hours / 24))
)
```

`!is.na(x)` says whether a value is observed. `&` combines conditions
entry by entry. For a missing value, `FALSE & NA` is `FALSE`. Dividing hours
by 24 changes units to days. It does not change event identity.

**If your answer differed, the likely cause is** using `<` instead of `<=` for
12, or leaving the response's missing-value rule implicit. The expected vector
is `TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE`; the response flag uses an explicit missing-value
rule.

</details>

### Summarize only when the row meaning should change {#summary}

**Slide cues:** “Summarize Last” and “Check Group Accounting”.

```{r}
#| label: issue-summary
issue_summary <- events_analysis |>
  group_by(issue) |>
  summarize(
    n_events = n(),
    observed_responses = sum(!is.na(response_hours)),
    mean_response_hours = mean(response_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    within_target_rate = mean(within_12_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n_events), issue)

stopifnot(
  nrow(issue_summary) == 4,
  sum(issue_summary$n_events) == nrow(events_analysis),
  sum(issue_summary$observed_responses) == 9,
  all(issue_summary$within_target_rate >= 0),
  all(issue_summary$within_target_rate <= 1)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: formatted-output-1
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(issue_summary, digits = 6)
```

There are now four rows because a row represents an issue category. Nine
summary rows would be the wrong invariant. The HVAC mean can be checked by
hand: `(4.5 + 11 + 9) / 3 = 24.5 / 3` hours. Access has two events,
with mean `(25 + 14) / 2 = 19.5` hours.

`mean(within_12_hours)` treats `TRUE` as 1 and `FALSE` as 0. Its denominator
is **all event rows in the category**. `mean(response_hours, na.rm = TRUE)`
uses only observed response times. In this file all times are observed, so
the two counts agree. With all times missing, that mean would be `NaN`;
the function in Meeting 2 explicitly rejects such a selected group.

**Predict · Think first:** is the overall target rate the unweighted mean
of the four category rates? Explain your denominator.

<details>
<summary>Check the denominator</summary>

No. HVAC has three events, while each other category has two. Five of the nine
events meet the rule, so the overall fraction is `5/9`, about 0.556. The
unweighted mean `(1 + 0 + 0 + 1)/4 = 0.5` gives each category equal weight,
answering a different question.

**If your answer differed, the likely cause is** giving each category equal
weight even though the categories contain different numbers of events.

```{r}
#| label: denominator-check
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(mean(events_analysis$within_12_hours), 5 / 9)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    weighted.mean(issue_summary$within_target_rate, issue_summary$n_events),
    5 / 9
  ))
)
```

</details>

### Close Meeting 1

**Slide cue:** “Meeting 1 Exit Ticket”.

Save, restart R, and rerun the completed blocks from the beginning. Explain one
assertion and a defect it could catch. A silent `stopifnot` means its conditions
passed. Match each assertion to the specific promise it checks.

**Individual in-class exit, final five minutes:** where should the event-analysis
pipeline pause for a named checkpoint, and why? Name the stage, say what one row
represents there, and describe one check and the problem it could reveal.
Two or three sentences; code is optional. Submit only through the announced
classroom route. The companion does not collect responses.

**Self-check (no submission):** your cleaned table has nine rows and nine
distinct IDs, but `EVT-009` has been replaced with a new ID, `EVT-010` (absent
from the supplied CSV). At which stage would you check, and what comparison
would reveal the replacement? Would that check also fail if the original rows
were merely reordered? Close earlier reveals and explain from memory before
opening the model answer.

<details>
<summary>Compare the Meeting 1 self-check</summary>

Check immediately after cleaning, while a row still represents one service
event. Compare the original and cleaned ID sets with `setequal`; it returns
`FALSE` because one original ID disappeared and another appeared. Counts and
uniqueness alone pass in this case. Keep those checks too, because they test
different promises. Merely reordering the original rows leaves `setequal`
true: it compares the IDs present, not their order.

</details>
